name: Flywheel training

card.summary: Flywheel training uses the inertia of a spinning wheel as resistance, loading the lowering phase of each rep to build muscle and strength.
card.aka: inertial training, isoinertial training, eccentric overload training, kBox
card.note: Machines are specialised equipment; technique and braking at the end of each rep matter.

quick.overview:
Flywheel training is a form of resistance training in which a strap wound around a spinning flywheel provides the load. Instead of gravity pulling on a weight, the lifter's own effort spins the wheel, and the wheel's inertia then resists as it winds back, which means the lowering (eccentric) phase of the rep can be loaded more heavily.

The payoff for physique is the same as other resistance training: more muscle and strength over time. A 2017 meta-analysis of nine randomised trials with 276 participants found flywheel eccentric-overload training produced larger gains than conventional training, and Wikipedia says current evidence suggests superiority for strength, power and hypertrophy.
quick.how: Lifters use flywheel devices such as the kBox for squats, rows, curls and other movements, pulling the strap to spin the wheel and resisting as it returns. The load scales with effort and wheel inertia rather than a fixed weight. Athletes, rehabilitation patients and astronauts have all used the method.
quick.risks: Flywheel work is generally used in supervised settings. Maximal eccentric efforts can cause muscle soreness, and braking technique is part of safe use. Studies in athletes with tendon problems have used it as a rehabilitation tool.

lead: Flywheel training is a strength method in which resistance comes from the inertia of a spinning flywheel rather than from gravity, as with free weights. Because the flywheel resists variably through the range of motion, it enables isoinertial training and eccentric overload, where the muscle is loaded during the lowering phase.[1]

For appearance, flywheel training is a way to build muscle. Wikipedia says it may improve strength, power, hypertrophy, muscle activation, muscle length and tendon stiffness, and that current evidence suggests it is superior to gravity-based training for increasing strength, power and hypertrophy.[1] More muscle and tendon capacity can then support more training and a fuller, stronger physique over time.

The method has a research history: an early 1924 study by Hansen and Lindhard at the University of Copenhagen, and 1990s work at the Karolinska Institute funded by NASA and ESA to counter muscle and bone loss in astronauts. Later studies extended to youth, professional athletes and older adults.[1] Commercial devices such as the kBox spread through European sport in the 2010s.[7]

chain: Spinning flywheel resists on the way back
Eccentric phase is loaded harder than with plain weights
More muscle and strength over training weeks
angle.text: Flywheel devices are used to train muscle with eccentric overload. Meta-analytic data link the method to muscle size and strength gains, which is how it contributes to physique.

infobox: Device flown on STS-78 in 1996; flywheel-based ARED on the ISS in 2009 [7]

paras: A rope or strap wound on a rotating flywheel is pulled during the lifting phase; as the wheel keeps spinning it rewinds the strap and the lifter resists, loading the eccentric phase. Resistance changes through the range of motion, unlike a fixed weight.[1]

In physical terms, effort in the pulling phase converts muscular work into rotational kinetic energy stored in the wheel; the stored energy is returned as the strap rewinds, so the harder the lifter pulls, the more the wheel resists on the return. The inertia of the wheel, set by the mass and arrangement of attached discs, determines the load scale, and the resistance accommodates to the lifter's effort rather than staying fixed.[7] Eccentric forces are often described as 20 to 50 percent above concentric forces in this setup.[7]

Horizontal units such as the Exxentric kBox suit linear movements like squats and pulls; vertical units such as the Desmotec D11 and VersaPulley allow multi-plane movement. Belt-driven systems are common in portable units, and rope-driven systems offer customisable resistance for team sports. Portable options such as the Wheeler YoYo and HandyGym suit rehabilitation and travel, while fixed units such as the 1080 Motion and kBox Pro are used in gyms and professional settings. Velocity sensors and inertia kits are sold as accessories.[7] Wikipedia illustrates the method with a kBox thruster exercise.[1]

Wikipedia dates early work to a 1924 Copenhagen study of maximum elbow-flexor work. In the 1990s, Karolinska researchers funded by NASA and ESA studied flywheel resistance exercise for astronauts in microgravity.[1] Grokipedia credits Per Tesch and H.E. Berg with an early flywheel ergometer, reports that the device flew on STS-78 in 1996, and says a flywheel-based Advanced Resistive Exercise Device was installed on the International Space Station in 2009.[7]

Sports adoption followed: the kBox launched in 2011, and use spread through European soccer clubs and elite programs in the 2010s and 2020s.[7] Research widened to youth athletes, handball and basketball players, fencers and older adults, and rehabilitation commentary appeared for musculoskeletal injury.[1]

Programmes described in general terms involve a few sets of several repetitions, two to three sessions a week, across 8 to 12 weeks. Heavier flywheel inertia is associated with strength and hypertrophy goals, and lighter inertia with speed and power; sessions often start with light warm-up repetitions and may combine flywheel and free-weight exercises.[7] Technique matters at the end of each rep, where the lifter must brake the returning wheel under control.[7]

The 2026 ACSM overview of reviews reports that resistance training in general improves muscle strength, size, power and function compared with no exercise, a baseline for all resistance methods.[2] A 2026 meta-analysis of advanced resistance systems in recreationally trained adults pooled 23 studies and found a small advantage over traditional multiple-set training for strength outcomes and a small, non-significant one for hypertrophy.[8]

Flywheel-specific studies include a randomised trial in 42 athletes with patellar tendinopathy comparing flywheel with heavy slow resistance training,[4] a 2003 controlled trial of hamstring injuries in elite soccer players after preseason eccentric-overload work,[5] a randomised trial in young soccer players of effects on strength, sprint and agility,[6] and reviews of eccentric training in team-sport athletes and of flywheel training in older adults.[9][10] A 2023 randomised trial compared eccentric-oriented with traditional strength training in the late stage of rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction in professional team-sport players.[11]

Grokipedia reports effect sizes across the literature of 1.33 for maximal strength, 1.19 for power and 0.59 for hypertrophy, a vertical jump improvement of about 6.8 percent, and notes limitations of small samples, few female and adolescent participants and few trials longer than 35 weeks.[7]

Flywheel work is generally described as a supervised method. Maximal eccentric efforts can cause muscle soreness, and sources recommend a neutral spine, controlled deceleration, low inertia for beginners and regular checks of belts and ropes.[7] Eccentric overload is also discussed as a mechanism of injury in some tendon ruptures, such as distal biceps injuries.[12]

A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport pooled nine randomised trials with 276 subjects and 92 effect sizes of flywheel eccentric-overload training in athletes and healthy people. The pooled standardised mean difference was 0.63 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.76), with no significant heterogeneity, and the analysis reported significant differences between flywheel and conventional resistance training.[3]
A randomised trial in 42 athletes with long-standing patellar tendinopathy compared inertial flywheel with heavy slow resistance training for pain and function.[4]
A 2017 meta-analysis note: the pooled estimate covered concentric and eccentric strength, muscle power, hypertrophy and vertical jump height.[3]

lore.intro: In strength communities, flywheel training is discussed within the wider topic of eccentric overload, alongside motorised machines and slow-lowering methods.[13]

claims.claim: Flywheel devices give true eccentric overload that plain weights cannot
claims.believers: Forum posters note motorised and inertial machines can provide eccentric overload in a way ordinary resistance stacks do not.[13]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes flywheel resistance as varying through the range and enabling eccentric overload.[1]

claims.claim: Flywheel training builds more muscle than conventional lifting
claims.believers: Advocates cite the 2017 meta-analysis favouring flywheel training.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says evidence suggests superiority for hypertrophy,[1] while a 2026 meta-analysis of advanced systems found hypertrophy differences small and non-significant.[8]

claims.claim: Flywheel work reduces hamstring injuries in athletes
claims.believers: Sports practitioners point to a soccer study of preseason eccentric overload.[5]
claims.experts: The 2003 trial studied injury occurrence in elite soccer players; Grokipedia cites a fall from 67 to 20 percent in one programme.[5][7]

claims.believers: Physiotherapists use it for tendon problems.
claims.experts: A randomised trial compared flywheel with heavy slow resistance in patellar tendinopathy;[4] a 2026 network meta-analysis compared exercise options for the condition.[14]

claims.claim: It suits older adults and astronauts
claims.believers: Proponents note use in space and with older people.
claims.experts: Reviews cover older adults;[10] NASA and ESA funded flywheel work for astronauts.[1]
